t.takhirbaj tepe@38.1,62.1:
The Murghab river flows out of the mountains of Afghanistan and dies in the sands of the Karakum desert, and where it fans out into a delta lies the oasis of Merv, in what is now southern Turkmenistan. For thousands of years people have farmed here, building cities one beside another as rivers shifted and empires came and went. Takhirbaj Tepe is one of the oldest of these settlements, a mound in the northern part of the oasis dating back to the Bronze and Iron Ages, long before the great medieval city that made Merv famous. It forms part of the State Historical and Cultural Park Ancient Merv, listed by UNESCO in 1999, alongside sites such as Yaz Tepe and Gobekli Tepe nearby.

Merv reached its peak in the twelfth century as a capital of the Seljuk empire, and by some accounts was one of the largest cities in the world at the time. In 1221 it was destroyed by the Mongols, with a massacre so terrible that the city never fully recovered. Today, the vast site is a landscape of crumbling mud walls, mounds and monuments: the great mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar with its double dome, the strange corrugated walls of the Kyz Kala fortresses, and walls stretching for miles across the desert.

Turkmenistan is one of the most closed countries in the world, and travel there needs serious planning. Tourist visas usually require a letter of invitation and a guide, while many overland travellers on motorbikes use a short transit visa, which forces a tight schedule. Check current rules well in advance. Fuel is cheap, though not always easy to find off the main roads, and roads vary from new highways to badly broken stretches with deep potholes.

The landscape is flat and dusty, with cotton fields, irrigation channels and desert. Summers are fiercely hot, often well above forty degrees, while winters can be cold, with occasional snow. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for a visit.

The nearest city is Mary, the modern successor to Merv, with fuel, hotels and markets. Try plov, rice cooked with meat and carrots, or shashlik grilled over coals, and drink green tea, which is offered everywhere and helps in the heat. Carry plenty of water when exploring the site.
t.besh agyz koshk@37.9,62.1:
Out on the edge of the Merv oasis in southeastern Turkmenistan, where irrigated fields fade into the sand of the Karakum desert, stand the ruins of buildings known as koshks. These were fortified mansions of mud brick, with heavily ribbed walls that look like giant corrugated cardboard, built in the early medieval period by the landed gentry of Merv. Besh Agyz, which means five mouths, is one of them, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of the Silk Roads, alongside the vast ruined cities of Ancient Merv, a World Heritage Site since 1999. Merv was for centuries one of the great cities of the Islamic world and a key stop on the routes between China and the Mediterranean, until the Mongols destroyed it in the thirteenth century.

The ruins are fragile, eroded by wind and the occasional rain, and their sheer size and isolation give them a haunting beauty. At Merv itself, the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, a twelfth-century Seljuk ruler, rises over the plain with its great dome, and the walls of successive cities stretch for kilometres. The desert light at sunrise and sunset is extraordinary, turning the mud brick pink and gold.

Riding in Turkmenistan is a serious undertaking. Entry with a vehicle requires visas, permits and often a guide, and rules can change without notice, so research carefully and plan well in advance. The roads range from new highways to broken tarmac and sand tracks, and police checkpoints are frequent. The climate is extreme: summer temperatures can exceed forty-five degrees, while winter nights can drop below freezing. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable times to visit.

Bayramaly, about thirty-five kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel and basic services, and Mary, the regional centre, is a little further. Fuel is cheap, but quality can vary and stations may be far apart, so carry spare fuel and plenty of water. Turkmen cuisine is hearty: plov, rice with meat and carrots, shashlik and fresh bread from the clay ovens. Be respectful of local customs, and always ask before taking photographs of people.
t.mausoleum of huday nazar the mausolea of:
The oasis of Merv, in south-eastern Turkmenistan, was for centuries one of the great cities of Central Asia, a stop on the Silk Road and at one point, under the Seljuks in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, possibly one of the largest cities in the world. Today its ruins are spread over a vast area of desert and farmland near the town of Bayramaly, and they form the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Ancient Merv. Scattered among them are small mausolea, tombs of holy men and companions of the Prophet, and the Mausoleum of Huday Nazar is one of these, a modest brick structure that has long been a place of local pilgrimage.

Merv's history spans more than two thousand years, with successive cities built side by side as the river shifted and rulers changed. Erk Kala, the oldest, dates back to the Achaemenid period; Gyaur Kala was the Sasanian and early Islamic city; and Sultan Kala was the Seljuk capital, dominated by the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, a massive domed building that still stands. The Mongols destroyed the city in 1221, and it never fully recovered.

Travelling in Turkmenistan is complicated. The country requires visas that are difficult to obtain, and independent travel is restricted; most visitors travel with an approved guide. Riding a motorcycle here requires careful planning and permits. The roads are a mixture of good highways and rough tracks, and the desert heat in summer is extreme, often above forty degrees. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild temperatures and clear skies. Sandstorms can occur.

Bayramaly, about twenty kilometres away, and Mary, the regional capital, have fuel and services. Fuel in Turkmenistan has historically been very cheap. Local food includes plov, rice with meat and carrots, and shashlik, grilled meat skewers, served with flat bread baked in clay ovens. Visiting the mausolea of Merv, with pilgrims tying cloth strips to nearby trees and the silence of the desert all around, is a strange and moving experience, a reminder of how great cities can return to dust.
t.thulli koshk@37.9,62.3:
Koshk is the local word for a fortified house, and around the oasis of Merv, in south-eastern Turkmenistan, dozens of these buildings survive from the early medieval period. Thulli koshk is one of them, a mud-brick structure with walls built in a distinctive corrugated pattern, like the folds of a curtain, which made them both stronger and more striking. These buildings were probably the homes of wealthy landowners, built to defend against raids, with rooms on two floors around a central hall.

The koshks of Merv date mostly from the Sasanian and early Islamic periods, between the sixth and tenth centuries, and the most famous is the Great Kyz Kala, near the ancient city of Gyaur Kala, whose corrugated walls still rise impressively above the plain. Thulli koshk lies further from the main sites, in the desert farmland of the oasis, and it is rarely visited. The ruins of Merv, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, cover a vast area, with cities from different periods side by side.

Travelling in Turkmenistan requires a visa, which can be difficult to obtain, and tourists usually travel with a licensed guide. Riding a motorcycle here is possible but requires careful planning and permits. The roads around Merv are a mixture of paved highways and dirt tracks through the oasis, and the desert heat in summer is extreme. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild temperatures. Dust storms can occur, and water should always be carried.

Bayramaly, about thirty-six kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and services, and Mary, the regional capital, has more. Fuel has historically been very cheap in Turkmenistan. The local food includes plov, shashlik and fresh bread, and green tea is drunk throughout the day. The Turkmen are known for their carpets and their horses, the famous Akhal-Teke, with their shimmering coats. Standing in front of a koshk, with its corrugated walls glowing in the evening light and the desert all around, is a strange and moving experience.
t.bahouddin naqshband architectural comple:
Bahauddin Naqshband died in 1389 in the village where he was born, a short ride from Bukhara, and the Sufi order that bears his name went on to spread across Central Asia, India, the Ottoman Empire and beyond. The Naqshbandi order emphasised silent remembrance of God and living a spiritual life within the everyday world, and its founder's tomb became one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Central Asia, so much so that locals sometimes call it the Mecca of Central Asia. The complex, with its mosques, minaret, courtyards and the tomb itself, was largely built in the sixteenth century under the Shaybanid rulers and restored in recent decades.

Pilgrims come from across Uzbekistan and beyond, walking around the tomb, praying, touching the old mulberry tree and drinking from the sacred well. The atmosphere is devout but welcoming, and visitors are generally received with courtesy, though modest dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered and head scarves for women in some areas.

Bukhara, about ten kilometres away, is one of the great cities of the Silk Road, its historic centre listed by UNESCO, with madrasas, mosques, minarets, covered bazaars and the fortress of the Ark. The Kalyan minaret, built in the twelfth century, so impressed Genghis Khan that he is said to have spared it when he destroyed much of the city. Spending a few days in Bukhara is one of the joys of travelling in Central Asia.

The riding in this part of Uzbekistan is flat, with long straight roads across irrigated fields, desert and villages. Surfaces vary, traffic can be unpredictable and police checkpoints are frequent. A practical point: many Uzbek cars run on compressed gas, and petrol of higher octane grades can be hard to find, so fill up whenever you see good fuel and plan your route around larger stations. Kagan, about eight kilometres away, and Bukhara have the most reliable options.

Food is a highlight: plov, the national dish of rice, meat and carrots, samsa baked in clay ovens, shashlik, fresh bread and endless pots of green tea. April and October are the sweet months. Summer heat in Bukhara is intense. Visit the complex in the early morning, when pilgrims gather in the cool and the call to prayer drifts over the courtyards.
t.historic centre of bukhara@39.8,64.4:
Bukhara is a city that feels like a lived-in museum. For more than two thousand years it has been a trading town on the routes across Central Asia, and in the ninth and tenth centuries, under the Samanid dynasty, it was one of the great centres of Islamic learning, home to scholars such as Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna. Genghis Khan sacked it in 1220, but the Kalyan Minaret, built in 1127, survived, and legend says even the conqueror was impressed. Today the old city is a remarkable ensemble of mosques, madrasas, caravanserais and domed bazaars, and it entered the World Heritage list in 1993.

The heart of the old town is the Lyabi-Hauz, a pool surrounded by mulberry trees and teahouses, flanked by madrasas and a khanaqah. Nearby, the trading domes, built in the sixteenth century, still house shops selling carpets, ceramics, knives and silk. The Ark fortress, the residence of the emirs, rises on its mound to the northwest, and the tiny Samanid Mausoleum, one of the oldest Islamic buildings in Central Asia, is a masterpiece of brickwork. The city has a slow, warm rhythm, especially in the evenings, when families gather around the pool.

For riders, Bukhara is an oasis in a vast, flat landscape. The roads in and out cross cotton fields, irrigated farmland and stretches of desert, and they are long, straight and sometimes rough. The main highway east toward Samarkand has been upgraded in places, but surfaces can vary, and there are many police checkpoints. Traffic includes slow trucks, horse carts and drivers who seem to have their own rules. Summer temperatures often exceed forty degrees, so spring and autumn are the best times to visit, when the days are warm and the evenings cool.

Bukhara is a city of about a quarter of a million people, with fuel, restaurants and accommodation, including many guesthouses in old merchants' houses. Fuel quality and availability can be an issue in Uzbekistan, and many vehicles run on gas, so fill up whenever you can. Local food includes plov, the rice dish cooked with meat, carrots and spices, and samsa baked in tandoor ovens. Park the bike securely at your guesthouse, walk the old city on foot, and sit by the pool with a pot of green tea as the sun goes down.
t.chor bakh necropolis@39.8,64.3:
A short ride west of Bukhara, in the village of Sumitan, a complex of courtyards, mosques and family tombs sits behind high walls, with blue-tiled portals rising above the surrounding houses. This is Chor Bakr, a necropolis built around the grave of Abu Bakr Said, a descendant of the Prophet who died in the tenth century. In the sixteenth century, the Shaybanid rulers of Bukhara built a memorial complex here, with a khanaqah, a mosque and a madrasa, and the cemetery became a resting place for the powerful Juybari sheikhs, a dynasty of religious leaders with great influence over the khanate. The name means "four brothers", referring to the four Abu Bakrs said to be buried here.

The complex has a strange, calm atmosphere. Its layout is like a city of the dead, with streets and walled courtyards containing family tombs, and the buildings are decorated with glazed tiles and carved wooden doors. It is a place of pilgrimage for local people, who come to pray and to ask for blessings, so visitors should dress modestly and behave respectfully. The setting, among trees and gardens on the edge of the village, makes it a peaceful break from the bustle of Bukhara.

The ride from Bukhara is short and flat, through the western suburbs and then along a road lined with irrigated fields, mulberry trees and village houses. Traffic is moderate, but watch for donkey carts, bicycles, livestock and children. Surfaces vary from decent asphalt to rough patches with potholes. The landscape is part of the Zeravshan river oasis, where irrigation has turned the desert into fertile land for centuries. Dust can be an issue on windy days, and summer heat is extreme, so ride in the morning or late afternoon.

Fuel and services are best found in Bukhara, about eight kilometres away. The village has small shops and perhaps a chaikhana, a teahouse, where you can get tea and bread. Remember that petrol supplies in Uzbekistan can be unreliable, so keep your tank topped up. Take your time inside the complex, walk the narrow streets between the tombs, and look at the tile work and the carved doors. Then sit in the shade for a while before heading back into the city.
The Merv oasis in southern Turkmenistan was once one of the greatest cities of the medieval world. Watered by the Murghab river, which flows north from Afghanistan and fans out into the Karakum desert, it was a capital of the Seljuk sultans in the eleventh and twelfth centuries and a key stop on the Silk Road. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221, and the ruins of successive cities, spread over a huge area, now form the Ancient Merv archaeological park, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1999. Among the ruins stand several mausolea of revered figures, small domed buildings that have drawn pilgrims for centuries and still do today.

The most famous monument at Merv is the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, a huge domed structure built in the twelfth century, which still stands proud above the plain. Around it lie the walls of the city of Sultan Kala, the older mounds of Erk Kala and Gyaur Kala, and the strange corrugated walls of the koshks, fortified mansions with ribbed facades that look like giant folded paper. Local people visit the shrines to pray, tie cloth to trees, and make offerings, and there is a strong sense of continuity between past and present.

Riding in Turkmenistan is a challenge, mostly for bureaucratic reasons. Independent travel is heavily restricted, visas are difficult to obtain, and tourists are usually required to travel with a guide, though transit visas are sometimes granted for overland travellers. Roads in the Mary region are flat and straight, with long stretches through cotton fields and desert, and surfaces that range from good to terrible. Police checkpoints are frequent. Summer heat is extreme, often well over forty degrees, so spring and autumn are the only sensible seasons.

The town of Bayramaly, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel and basic services, and the regional capital Mary, further west, is larger. Fuel is cheap, but quality can vary. Bring plenty of water to Merv, because the site is large, exposed and dusty, and there is little shade. Food in the region is simple: plov, grilled meats, bread and melons, which are excellent in late summer. Take your time among the ruins and shrines, and let the scale of the place sink in. A great city stood here, and the desert has slowly reclaimed it.
t.bairam ali ding@37.8,62.1:
North of Bayramaly, toward the edge of the irrigated land of the Merv oasis, the remains of a ding stand on the flat plain: a fortified building of mud brick, often square or rectangular, with thick walls and corner towers, used as a manor, a refuge or a watch post. The oasis is scattered with structures like this, from medieval times to the more recent past, and many are associated with the defence of farmland and water channels against raiders from the desert. They are part of the wider archaeological landscape of Merv, one of the richest in Central Asia, where every mound and wall has a story, even if not all of them have been told yet.

The Murghab river, the lifeline of the oasis, splits into countless channels here, feeding cotton fields, orchards and villages. Beyond the fields, the Karakum desert begins abruptly, a sea of sand and scrub that covers most of Turkmenistan. The light is harsh and bright, the dust fine and pervasive, and the horizon seems endless. In spring, the desert edge blooms briefly with wildflowers and tulips, and the birdlife along the canals can be surprisingly rich.

Riding here is a matter of straight roads and long distances. The routes north of Bayramaly are flat and largely empty, crossing farmland and then semi-desert, with surfaces that can deteriorate quickly into potholes, sand drifts and gravel. Navigation can be tricky, as signs are few and maps not always reliable. Remember that travel in Turkmenistan is tightly controlled, and venturing off main routes without a guide or permission may lead to trouble with the authorities. Heat in summer is extreme, and sandstorms can blow up with little warning.

The nearest services are in Bayramaly, about sixteen kilometres away, which has fuel, shops and simple restaurants, and Mary, the regional capital, has more. Carry plenty of water and some food, because there is nothing out here. A stop at the ding is a chance to stand in the silence of the oasis edge, look at the crumbling mud walls, and imagine the people who sheltered here from raiders, heat and dust storms. It is not a polished tourist site, but it is real, and it has its own quiet power.
t.varakhsha settlement@39.9,64.1:
Thirty kilometres or so west of Bukhara, beyond the last irrigated fields, the land turns to sand and salt crust at the edge of the Kyzylkum desert, and here a low mound of eroded mud brick rises from the flat ground. This is Varakhsha, once a flourishing town and the residence of the Bukhar Khudats, the pre-Islamic rulers of the Bukhara oasis. It thrived in the early medieval centuries, when the oasis extended further than it does today, and was abandoned around the eleventh century, probably as irrigation failed and the desert advanced.

Soviet archaeologists excavating the site in the twentieth century found the remains of a palace with spectacular wall paintings: hunters riding elephants and fighting wild beasts, processions and decorative patterns, and carved stucco panels. The originals are in museums, and on site you will find only the weathered mounds, outlines of walls and a sense of utter emptiness. It is a place for imagination and for the silence of the desert.

Bukhara itself is one of the great cities of the Silk Road, a living museum of mosques, madrasas, minarets and covered bazaars. Its old centre is a World Heritage Site, and the Kalon minaret, which impressed even Genghis Khan, still dominates the skyline. Not far from the city is the Bahouddin Naqshband complex, the shrine of the founder of an important Sufi order, a major pilgrimage destination.

Riding to Varakhsha means leaving the asphalt behind, at least for the last stretch. Desert tracks can be sandy and soft, especially in summer, and getting stuck is a real possibility. Heat is the biggest challenge: from June to August, temperatures regularly exceed 40 degrees, and there is no shade. April, May, September and October are far kinder, with mild days and cool nights. Carry plenty of water, and let someone know where you are going.

Fuel in Uzbekistan can be tricky. Many vehicles run on gas, and petrol stations may have limited supplies of higher grades, so fill up when you can in Bukhara or Romitan, which is twenty-seven kilometres away. The food is a highlight: plov, the rice dish with meat and carrots, samsa baked in clay ovens, and fresh bread. A pot of green tea in a teahouse in Bukhara, with the sun going down behind the domes, washes the dust out of your throat better than anything.
t.nuestra senora de santa ana@-27.4,-55.6:
Deep in the red earth of Misiones, in the north-eastern tip of Argentina, the forest is slowly reclaiming a mission town. Nuestra Señora de Santa Ana was one of the Jesuit reductions, settlements where Jesuit priests gathered the Guaraní people in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, partly to protect them from slave raiders and partly to convert them. The towns were laid out around a central plaza with a church, a school, workshops and houses, and the Guaraní built, carved and played music in a form that mixed European baroque with their own skills. Santa Ana, founded in the 1630s, is among the lesser known, and much of it lies in ruin under trees and vines.

Walking through, you see the big stone walls of the church, the foundations of the workshops and the grid of the town, with roots from fig trees climbing the masonry. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, the missions emptied and the forest took over. The ruins of San Ignacio Miní, a short drive away, are better preserved and have a visitor centre, while Santa Ana is quieter, and the combination of silence, birdsong and red dust is a good reason to go.

Loreto and Cerro Corá are the nearby villages, both small, with a shop and a few places to eat, so do not count on fuel. Fill up in Posadas, the provincial capital, or in San Ignacio, and carry water. The main road here, Ruta 12, runs along the Paraná river with sweeping views of forests and yerba mate plantations, the leaves dried and sold across the country, and it is a good, smooth road for long, easy riding. Side roads are often dirt, and when it rains the red mud turns slick and heavy, so choose your days.

The climate is humid and subtropical, with hot summers, sudden storms and mosquitoes, and winters are mild but can be wet. April to October is the most comfortable season. Try a gourd of mate with the locals, and do not pass up chipá, a cheesy bread made from cassava flour, which you will find at roadside stalls.
t.mosque mausoleum of talkhattan baba@37.6:
The Karakum desert surrounds the oasis of Merv on three sides, and the Murghab river, which feeds the oasis, ends in the sand a little downstream. Talkhatan Baba, a brick mosque and mausoleum in the area of Mary, belongs to the medieval Islamic centuries when Merv was one of the great cities of the world, a Seljuk capital with libraries, observatories and a population that rivalled any in Europe.

It makes more sense seen with the rest of the region. The ancient cities of Merv, listed by UNESCO in 1999, spread across the plain in a series of walled enclosures from different eras, with the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, the Seljuk ruler, at the heart of it, and a huge fortress wall of mud brick that has weathered into soft shapes. The Mongols destroyed the city in 1221, and it never recovered, which is why so much is left untouched in the desert.

Practically, Turkmenistan is a difficult country for independent travellers. Visas are hard to obtain, a guide is usually required, and foreign vehicles are subject to heavy paperwork and fees, so most visitors travel with a licensed tour operator. If you can arrange it, the roads in the Mary region are straight and flat, with mile after mile of cotton fields, irrigation canals and desert scrub, and heat that can reach forty-five degrees in summer. Fuel is cheap, but the supply can be uneven, and you should take as much as you can. Bayramaly, a town of about seventy-five thousand, and Murgab, much smaller, have shops and basic services.

Spring and autumn are the only sensible seasons, with March and April bringing green fields and wildflowers on the steppe, and October giving mild days. Bring water, a hat and a lot of patience, and accept the tea that people offer.
t.kelleli adji kui taip@38.3,61.7:
Four thousand years ago, in the delta of the Murghab river, a civilisation grew up around irrigated fields and fortified settlements that archaeologists call Margiana, or the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex. Kelleli, Adji Kui and Taip are names of mounds in that delta, low hills of eroded mud brick standing in the flat plain of the Karakum, where the river once split into channels and watered an oasis. People lived here between about 2300 and 1700 BC, building walled compounds with towers, workshops, graves and what may have been temples with fire altars.

The famous excavations of this culture were carried out at Gonur Depe by the Soviet archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi, who believed he had found the place where the ritual drink haoma, mentioned in early Indo-Iranian texts, was prepared. Whether he was right is still argued, but the sheer scale of the settlements, planned, fortified and rich in metalwork, surprises anyone who expects the desert to be empty. The river shifted, the oasis dried and the people moved on, leaving the mounds to the sand.

The mounds are low, and the track to them may be soft or washed out, so go with a guide who knows the way. Turkmenistan requires visitors to travel with a licensed guide in most cases, and independent riding is difficult, with visas, vehicle permits and checkpoints to deal with. Plan well in advance.

The landscape itself is its own reward, with ripples of pale sand, saxaul bushes, flocks of sheep and the odd camel, under a huge sky. In midsummer the heat is dangerous, so choose spring or autumn, and carry more water than you think you need, and extra fuel, because there are no pumps in the sand. Nights are cold in winter, and sandstorms can appear without warning. When the evening light flattens the plain, the shape of the old walls shows up, and the past surfaces briefly.
t.akja gala caravanserai@38.1,62.6:
The Silk Road across the Karakum was never a single road. It was a series of wells, forts and caravanserais, a day's travel apart, where camels could drink and merchants could sleep behind walls. Akja Gala is one of these shelters, a square brick building with a central courtyard and rooms around it, set in sand and saxaul scrub between Merv and the Amu Darya, the river called the Oxus by the Greeks.

The route it served was a hard one. After Merv, caravans heading east crossed some two hundred kilometres of dry land to reach the Amu Darya at Amul, an ancient crossing and later the city of Chardzhou, now Turkmenabat. Water was the constant problem, and the caravanserais were built close to wells or to cisterns that stored rain. Travellers paid a toll, rested, fed their animals and carried on, and the stories and goods that moved through places like this shaped half of Asia.

Amul Settlement, the other half of this ride, is the old riverside site, and the contrast between the desert and the green belt along the Oxus is startling. Turkmenistan is difficult for independent riders, as a licensed guide is almost always required, and visas and vehicle permits take time and money. Tour operators can arrange a trip with a car and driver, and may know the track to remote sites.

The desert is a place of extremes. Summers are fiercely hot, with temperatures above forty-five degrees in the shade, and winters are cold, with frosts and bitter winds. Spring, with its short green carpet and flowers, and autumn are the times to go. Fuel and water are essential, since distances between settlements are long and the sand is soft off the road. Mary, the nearest city, has everything you need, but beyond it services are thin. A camel on the road is not a rarity, and the dust at dusk turns the sky orange.
t.konegala caravanserai@38.2,62.8:
What I can tell you is what a caravanserai was, because the answer explains the place. Along the Silk Road, travellers needed to eat, sleep and water their animals every day or two, and rulers and merchants built fortified inns at intervals along the way, with thick walls, a single gate, a central courtyard and small rooms around the edge for people, with stables and storerooms.

The desert here is vast, flat and quiet, with low dunes, saltbush, and in spring a thin carpet of green and red poppies that disappears by summer. The ruins that survive are made of mud brick or baked brick, and they weather quickly, so what stands today may be a fraction of the original. The ancient oasis city of Merv, a World Heritage site with the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, lies not far to the west, and gives an idea of the scale of the culture that built roads and inns across this country.

Anyone thinking of riding here needs to prepare carefully. Turkmenistan has strict entry requirements, visas are difficult to obtain, and independent travel is normally limited, with guides, itineraries and transit permits required for foreign visitors. Rules about motorcycles, border crossings and the use of cameras are subject to change, so check them with a specialist agency. Fuel is cheap, but supply can be uneven, and distances between towns are large. Heat in summer is extreme, often above forty degrees, so spring and autumn are the best seasons, and winter nights can be cold.

There is no town nearby that I can name with confidence, so plan to carry fuel, water, food and spares for the whole day. If you do get there, take it slowly, drink a lot, and let the silence of the place do its work.
Merv was one of the great cities of the world, and today it is a field of mud-brick walls in the Karakum desert. At its height in the twelfth century, under the Seljuk sultan Sanjar, Merv was among the biggest cities on Earth, a Silk Road oasis with libraries, mosques, markets and an elaborate water system fed by canals from the Murghab river. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221, and although a later city grew nearby, the old centre never recovered. The ancient cities of Merv, which spread across a series of walled sites from the time of the Persians to the fifteenth century, were inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1999.

Abdullah Khan Kala is one of the later sites, a fortified citadel of the Timurid period, built in the fifteenth century when Merv was revived under Shah Rukh, a son of Timur, with great mud-brick walls and towers still standing among the sand. A koshk, in Turkmen, is a fortified building or manor house, and the imaret, a word of Ottoman origin, is a kitchen or hospice, so the name suggests a charitable building near the fortress. Not far away, the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, a huge brick cube with a double dome, stands as the best-preserved building in the whole complex.

The landscape is pure desert, flat, dusty and enormous, with the horizon marked by crumbling walls and the thin green line of irrigated fields near the modern town of Bayramaly. Summer temperatures are extreme, with highs above forty degrees, and winters are cold and windy. Spring, with a thin carpet of green and flowers, and early autumn are the best times. The wind can blow dust across the road.

Riding in Turkmenistan is a formal business. Foreign visitors generally need a visa or a transit permit, and often a guide, and you need to arrange vehicle entry in advance, so careful planning and current information are essential. Fuel is cheap, but supplies are not always reliable, and stations can be far apart on desert roads. Bayramaly is a town of about seventy-five thousand, with services, and Mary, the regional capital, is nearby. Carry water, avoid the midday heat and respect any signs or guards at the site.
t.greater and lesser kiz kala@37.7,62.2:
Two squat, ribbed fortresses stand on the plain outside ancient Merv, and they have kept their purpose a mystery. Greater Kiz Kala and Lesser Kiz Kala, the Maiden Fortresses, are fortified buildings dating from the sixth to the seventh century AD, when Merv was a provincial capital of the Sasanian Persian Empire, and they are a fine example of the fortified country house of the period. The larger one is about thirty metres square, with massive walls, rounded corner towers, and a surface made of shallow vertical grooves and arrow slits that give it a corrugated look, and the smaller one stands a short distance away, built in much the same style.

The legend that gave them their name says that a king had two daughters, and each had her own fortress, though the stories are late and charming rather than historical. Archaeologists think that they were the residences of wealthy landowners, built for protection, a place to store crops and to shelter from raids by nomads. Inside the larger fortress there are rooms around a courtyard, a staircase, and the remains of a vaulted ceiling, and at its heart is a kind of tower. Local legends also say they were joined by a secret tunnel, though no tunnel has been found.

The setting adds to the effect. The two buildings stand alone in the flat, pale landscape beyond the main city walls of Merv, with irrigated fields, cotton and dusty tracks nearby, and the walls take on a pink and gold colour in the morning and evening light. In midsummer, the heat reflected from the clay is hard to endure, so visit early. Winter brings cold winds and occasional rain, which turns the ground to sticky mud.

The nearest town is Bayramaly, about four kilometres away, a city of about seventy-five thousand people with fuel and shops, and Mary is a bigger regional centre. Foreign riders must check in advance what is possible, as visas, guides and vehicle permits are tightly controlled. Take plenty of water and a hat, and look closely at the wall surfaces, since the patterns are the best part of the site.
t.state historical and cultural park ancie:
South of the Karakum and just outside the modern city of Mary, the ground is littered with the ghosts of cities. Nagym Kala, the Greater and Lesser forts, are two of the walled settlements that make up the old Merv oasis, one of the great cities of the Silk Road. The Murgab river spreads out here into a delta that has fed farmers for thousands of years, and Merv grew up where the water met the desert.

Merv was at various times the capital of a Persian satrapy, a Seljuk imperial city and a centre of learning that rivalled Baghdad and Nishapur. The Mongols sacked it in 1221, and the accounts of the slaughter are among the grimmest in the medieval record, though numbers in the chronicles are almost certainly exaggerated. What survives now are mud-brick walls, mausolea and the ruined fortresses of several different cities, built side by side as the centre shifted. UNESCO listed the site in 1999.

The ride is flat and hot. The roads run through irrigated cotton fields and canals, then out into low desert where the horizon is wide and the sky is huge. Expect rough patches of asphalt, livestock and slow vehicles, and a very strong sun between May and September. Turkmenistan is a tightly controlled country, and travelling by motorbike requires permits, a guide and careful planning. Check what is allowed before you go, because rules change and checkpoints are common.

Bayramaly, nine kilometres away, is a town of some size, and Mary, a bit further, is the regional capital with hotels and fuel. Between them they cover your needs. The best light for the ruins is early morning or late afternoon, when the walls turn the colour of honey and the heat drops. Bring a hat and a lot of water. Walking the walls of Greater Kyz Kala or the Sultan Sanjar mausoleum nearby gives a better sense of scale than any photo. It is an empty, quiet place, and its emptiness is the point.
t.yeradzhi@38.8,62.5:
Yeradzhi is a name on the map in the middle of the Karakum, the Black Sand desert that covers most of Turkmenistan. There is no town in the nearby list, which tells you most of what you need to know. The Karakum is one of the largest sand deserts in the world, with ridges, hollows, saxaul scrub and takyrs, the flat clay pans that bake hard in summer. It is cold in winter, brutally hot in summer, and when it rains the clay turns to grease.

The rides that start here connect to Repetek, which has a well-known desert reserve and research station, and to Thulli koshk, a ruined fortified house of the old caravan era. Repetek is famous for its saxaul forest and for the studies of desert wildlife that have been carried out there for decades. You may see lizards, tortoises and, with luck, gerbils at dusk. The old caravan routes crossed the desert between oases, with wells and fortified rest stops, and a ruin like Thulli koshk is a clue to how risky those journeys were.

This is serious country for a motorbike. Roads can be lonely, sand drifts onto the surface, and the nearest fuel may be a long way off. Turkmenistan has strict rules for foreign travellers, including guides, permits and approved routes, so plan this long before you land. Carry extra fuel if you are allowed to, extra water, and tell someone where you are going. Expect long distances between settlements and few places for food.

The reward is silence and space. The sand shifts from pale gold to rust through the day, and at dawn and dusk the light is low and warm. Wind is a factor, since it can carry sand across the road and reduce visibility. The best seasons are spring and autumn. In spring there may be a brief flush of green and flowers. Do not underestimate the heat or the scale, and treat this place with respect.
t.kurtly caravanserai@37.9,62.3:
Kurtly sits on the flat plain near Merv, in the south of the Karakum, and the caravanserai that gives the place its label is a reminder that the old Silk Road was a network of small stops as much as great cities. A caravanserai was a fortified inn where merchants and animals could rest, drink and sleep within walls, usually a day's travel from the next one. Some were grand, with arcades and domed rooms. Others were simple compounds of mud brick. Few survive intact, and the ones in Turkmenistan are often reduced to low walls and mounds.

Merv itself is about thirty kilometres away, and the surrounding region is the Murgab oasis, one of the oldest irrigated lands in Central Asia. The Murgab river dries into the desert here, and canals draw its water off to feed cotton and wheat. Local rides connect Kurtly with other sites, including the mosque and mausoleum of Talkhatan Baba, a mud-brick building from the eleventh century that is still a place of local pilgrimage, and the Kelte Minara, a short, stubby, tiled minaret.

The landscape is flat and almost treeless, with irrigation ditches, camels and sheep, and fields of cotton in summer. Roads are straight, the surface changes without warning, and the sun is hard from May to September. Wind blows dust across the road in dry weather. Bayramaly, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest big town and should have fuel and basic food, while Mary is the regional centre. In Turkmenistan, fuel is cheap by European standards but not always easy to find on rural roads, so fill up whenever you can.

Travel here needs planning, since foreign visitors normally need permits and a guide, and motorcycle rules may be strict. Check before you go. When you reach Kurtly, give yourself a few minutes to look at the walls and think about the people who rested here, tired, thirsty and probably worried about the next day's road. The place rewards silence and attention more than photographs. Late afternoon, with long shadows and cooler air, is the time to be here.
t.jesuit mission of jesus de tavarangue@-2:
The most striking thing about Jesus de Tavarangue is what is missing. The church tower is a rectangular stone shaft rising into the air with nothing attached; the great church it was meant for was never finished. In 1767 the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits from its territories, and the mission, which was in the middle of its final, grandest phase of construction, was abandoned. What remains is a handsome ruin of red sandstone, with arches, columns and carved details, set in a grassy plaza under the subtropical sky, silent and a little strange.

Jesus was one of thirty Jesuit missions, or reducciones, founded among the Guarani people in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, in a region that spans what is now Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil. The Jesuits gathered Guarani communities into planned towns with a central plaza, a church, workshops, schools and homes, and the Guarani became skilled musicians, sculptors, architects and craftsmen, producing baroque art with their own style. The missions were self-governing, prosperous and, according to many historians, a remarkable social experiment. Jesus and nearby Trinidad were listed by UNESCO in 1993.

Jesus lies in Itapua department in southern Paraguay, near the town of Hohenau, which was founded by German and Russian settlers in the early twentieth century and still keeps some of their influence. Trinidad, another mission, is only a short ride away, with a bigger, better-preserved church and wonderful stone carving. Encarnacion, on the Parana river facing Argentina, is the largest city nearby, with fuel, food and hotels.

Riding is easy but hot. Paved roads, such as Route 6, run through red-earth farmland with fields of soybeans, wheat and yerba mate, and the side roads are often dirt, which turns to sticky mud after rain. Fuel is available in the towns but sparse between them. Summers are fiercely hot and humid, with storms, so choose April to October for a more comfortable ride.

Guarani is still widely spoken in Paraguay, and it is an official language alongside Spanish. People drink tereré, cold mate with ice and herbs, from a shared cup, and a local bakery will sell chipa, a cheesy bread, still warm. Visit in the early morning, when the stone glows red and the heat has not yet arrived.
t.amul settlement@39.0,63.6:
Amul was the old name for the crossing that later became Türkmenabat, and the settlement sits only six kilometres from that modern city on the Amu Darya, the river the ancients called the Oxus. It is a flat, dusty place of low mounds and eroded walls, and you might drive past without noticing. What it marks is a ford on one of the great Silk Road routes, where caravans coming from Merv in the southwest met the river before heading on toward Bukhara.

In medieval times Amul, sometimes called Amul-i Shatt, the Amul on the riverbank, was a significant trading stop and fortress. Arab geographers describe its markets and its position on the road to Khorasan. Cities along the Amu Darya rose and fell with the river, which moves its bed across the plain; places left high and dry gradually died, and the mudbrick walls have since melted back into the earth. That is part of why this landscape feels so quiet: it is built from layers of vanished towns.

Riding out here means open desert roads. East and west of the river you will cross the Karakum, with long straight asphalt, stretches of washboard and shifting sand blown over the carriageway. Spring and autumn are comfortable; summers reach extreme heat and winters can be bitterly cold with sharp winds. Take more water than you think you need and watch for camels on the verge. Entering Turkmenistan involves visas, a transit or guide arrangement and registration, so plan it with care.

Türkmenabat, with a population of over two hundred thousand, is the practical stop and has fuel, shops and cafes. Petrol in Turkmenistan is cheap by European standards, though supply and rules for foreign vehicles change. Farap, about seventeen kilometres away, is smaller. Melons from this region are famous across Central Asia, and a slice of ripe melon in summer is a better reward than most rest stops.
t.abdullah khan kala@37.7,62.2:
Abdullah Khan Kala is a mud-brick fortress on the edge of the Merv oasis, about five kilometres from the town of Bayramaly, and it makes a surprising amount of noise for something so silent. Its walls are enormous, rising out of the flat desert plain, and from the top you can see the pale shapes of other Merv monuments far away, all of them made from the same earth.

Merv, at its height a city that rivalled Baghdad and Cairo, lies in a sprawl of separate walled cities built across more than two thousand years. Abdullah Khan Kala belongs to the late phase, when Timurid rulers rebuilt the area after the Mongol destruction of 1221, one of history's grimmest massacres. It is a square fortress that served as a garrison and a symbol, with high walls, corner towers and a single gate. It was not the biggest part of Merv, but it is among the best preserved, and the clay has weathered into soft ridges and creases.

The ride is flat and straight. From Mary, thirty-odd kilometres to the west, the road runs through irrigated cotton and wheat, then out onto desert where the verge disappears into sand. Expect heat from May to September, sometimes over forty degrees, and wind that raises dust. The best time to come is spring, when the plain is briefly green, or early autumn, with low gold light. Sunrise and sunset do wonders for the brickwork.

Bayramaly, with about seventy-five thousand people, is the nearest place for fuel and food, and Mary is the larger option. Take water and a hat, because there is almost no shade at the site, and bring a camera for the silhouettes. Foreigners travelling in Turkmenistan need visas and, usually, a guide or transit permit, so organise that ahead of time. Locals are friendly and curious, and melon sellers on the road deserve a stop.
t.yusuf hamdani@37.7,62.2:
The Yusuf Hamdani complex lies in the Merv oasis, just under seven kilometres from Bayramaly, among low walled courtyards and a handful of new-looking domes. Unlike most of Merv, which is ruin, this is a living shrine: pilgrims arrive from across Turkmenistan and beyond, women in colourful headscarves, men in lambskin hats, many tying cloth strips to trees and leaving small offerings.

Yusuf Hamdani, or Hamadani, was a twelfth-century Sufi master who was born in western Persia, studied in Baghdad and eventually settled in Merv, then a great centre of learning. He taught here, and his pupils carried his teachings across Central Asia, becoming the chain of masters that later produced the Naqshbandi order. Tradition says he died on a journey and was brought back to Merv for burial. The present mausoleum is a modern reconstruction on the old site, which is why the tiles and domes look so fresh against the older mud-brick ruins nearby.

The countryside here is flat and green close to the irrigation canals, then pale and bare in between. The road from Bayramaly is short, quiet and simple. Heat in summer is fierce, so aim for morning or evening, and in spring you may find pomegranate and apricot blossom in the gardens. Dress modestly, take your shoes off where asked, and ask before photographing people at prayer. Visitors are welcome if they show respect, and you may be offered tea.

Bayramaly is the nearest practical stop with fuel and cafes, and Mary, about thirty kilometres away, is bigger and has more choice of hotels. There is little in the way of services right at the site, so carry water. Foreign riders need the correct visas and, usually, guide or transit arrangements, and rules can change, so check close to your travel date. The surrounding mausolea of Imam Bakr and Shafi are close and make an easy second stop in the same morning.
t.santa maria la mayor@-27.9,-55.3:
Red earth is the first thing you notice in Misiones, the thin finger of northeastern Argentina squeezed between Paraguay and Brazil. The soil is the colour of a brick, the forest is subtropical, and the roads cut through it leave long scarlet stripes on the verge. Santa María la Mayor, a small town of under two thousand, lies in this country, and its main attraction is a ruin the forest nearly swallowed.

It was one of the Jesuit reductions, the mission towns set up among the Guaraní people in the seventeenth century. The Society of Jesus founded Santa María la Mayor in 1626, and over the following century dozens of such settlements grew across what is now Argentina, Paraguay and Brazil, each with a plaza, a church, workshops, schools, fields and cattle. Music mattered, and Guaraní craftsmen carved sculptures and played European instruments with a skill that astonished visitors. When the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767, the towns declined, and many were left to the jungle. What remains at Santa María is part of the UNESCO listing of the Jesuit Missions of the Guaraníes, with red sandstone walls, the outline of the plaza and a small museum with carved stones.

Riding here is gentle and humid. Roads are mostly paved and quiet, with big skies, red dirt shoulders, fields of yerba mate, the shrub whose leaves are dried and drunk as the national infusion, and patches of tall forest where toucans sometimes cross. The heat in summer is heavy, and sudden tropical downpours turn dirt tracks into slippery red clay, so avoid unpaved side roads after rain. Livestock, dogs and slow tractors are common on the road, and nighttime riding is best avoided.

Fuel is the practical question. Santa María is small, and the larger towns of Apóstoles, to the south, and Posadas, the provincial capital on the Paraná river, are the reliable places to fill up. A thermos of hot water and a gourd of mate is the local way to wait out a storm, and roadside stalls often sell chipa, a baked cheese bread that is a staple of the region.

Visit in the cooler months of April to September, when the air is dry and the light is soft.
t.historic urban centre of the merv oasis@:
Merv is what is left of a city that once argued with Baghdad about which of them was the greatest in the Muslim world. Today it lies as a wide spread of mud-brick walls, domes and mounds in the Karakum desert of Turkmenistan, a few kilometres from the town of Bayramaly and not far from the regional capital Mary. The Murgab river fans out here into an oasis, and for more than two thousand years that thin green strip made Merv the natural halt on the Silk Road between Persia and Central Asia.

There is not one Merv but several, laid side by side as each new ruler built next to the old. The oldest walls, Erk Kala, go back to the Achaemenid era. Alongside stand Gyaur Kala of the Sasanian and early Islamic age, and the later Sultan Kala, the capital of the Seljuk sultans in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar is the building most visitors cannot miss, a big brick cube that was once crowned by a double dome and has been a landmark in the flat plain for nearly nine hundred years. Then came 1221, when Mongol forces took the city and killed a huge share of its people, a blow from which Merv never fully recovered. Kyz Kala, the smaller fortified buildings with their ribbed mud walls, are the ones that look best in low light.

Treat the ride as an expedition rather than a joyride. Turkmenistan requires foreign travellers to arrange visas and often permits, and motorcycle entry takes planning ahead, so do the paperwork long before you arrive. The roads across the Karakum are flat, long and straight, with heat above forty degrees in summer and a wind that carries sand across the tarmac. Spring and autumn are far kinder. Fuel is strikingly cheap in this country, but stations are spread out, so fill up in Mary or Bayramaly and carry water.

At the site, the ground is dust and fragments of glazed pottery, and the best hour is early or at sunset when the brick turns gold. Take shade, go slowly, and look for the wind-carved edges where whole streets are buried only a metre down.
t.port au choix@50.7,-57.4:
Port au Choix sits at the tip of a low, flat peninsula on Newfoundland's Great Northern Peninsula, where the Viking Trail, Route 430, runs along the coast of the Gulf of St Lawrence. It is a working fishing town with colourful houses, stacks of lobster pots and boats drawn up on the shore, and it has a surprising depth of history. The Port au Choix National Historic Site preserves the remains of some of the oldest settlements in the region, with burial grounds used by the Maritime Archaic people about four thousand years ago, and later by Dorset Palaeo-Eskimo groups. The graves contained tools, ornaments and spiritual objects, giving a rare glimpse into a prehistoric culture.

The landscape is stark and beautiful. The peninsula is covered in limestone barrens, where harsh conditions have produced a rare collection of arctic and alpine plants, which bloom in a short burst of colour in early summer. The Point Riche lighthouse stands at the end of the road, with views over the sea, and on a clear day the Labrador coast can be seen across the strait. Seabirds and whales pass offshore, and in spring icebergs sometimes drift past.

For riders, this is a long, rewarding road. Route 430 follows the coast for hundreds of kilometres, with long straights and gentle curves, wide skies and few other vehicles. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves can make the road rough, especially after winter. The great danger is moose. Newfoundland has a huge moose population, and collisions are common, especially at dawn and dusk, so ride cautiously and avoid night riding.

Port au Choix has fuel, a small supermarket and a few places to eat, but services are limited in the evening, and the distances between settlements are long, so fill the tank when you can. Fog and wind are frequent, and the temperature can be cold even in summer. Gros Morne National Park lies to the south, and the Viking settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows lies far to the north. Bring warm clothing and patience, and you will be rewarded.
t.nevyansk@57.5,60.2:
There is a tower in Nevyansk that has been leaning for three hundred years, and nobody can say for sure whether it was meant to. It was built in the early 1720s for Akinfiy Demidov, the ironmaster who ran the Nevyansk works after his father Nikita, and it stands about fifty-seven metres high, a white brick stack of several tiers with a clock and a spire. The top leans visibly away from the vertical, by a couple of metres, which makes it one of the more famous curiosities of the Urals. Stories swirl around it: that it held a secret room for forging silver coins, that the iron roof carries a lightning rod older than Benjamin Franklin's, and that a whisper at one corner can be heard at the opposite one. Some of this is local legend. What is certain is that it was part of the Demidov industrial empire, which fed the army and the building of Saint Petersburg.

Nevyansk itself is a small industrial town of twenty-five thousand, about eighty kilometres north-west of Yekaterinburg, on the Neyva River, with an old works pond at its heart. The Demidov ironworks created it in 1700s, and the Old Believers, who fled persecution and found work here, helped to create a distinctive school of icon painting. The Nevyansk icons, with their detailed gold and fine drawing, are found in museums, and the town has a good one with a collection of them.

For riding, the area is gentle. The roads from Yekaterinburg run through low hills and forest, with long straights and easy bends, and the traffic is moderate, with trucks and commuters. The surface is usually decent, but watch for frost damage and potholes after winter. In summer, the roads are warm and the forest smells of resin. September is golden, and snow comes early. The Urals here are old and low, so views are modest, but the countryside is pleasant.

Fuel and food are easy in town, which has several stations, a supermarket and a few cafés. Nizhny Tagil to the north and Kirovgrad to the west are bigger centres, and a ring of ponds and old ironworks villages lies between them.

Look up at the tower from the foot, and judge the angle for yourself. It is worth the detour, if only for the sheer improbability.
t.nizhny tagil@57.9,60.0:
Nizhny Tagil is an iron city, and it has been one since Peter the Great's day. In 1702, a Tula blacksmith named Nikita Demidov was given the Nevyansk works, and his family soon spread across the Urals, founding Tagil in 1722 on the river of the same name. The Demidov family grew into one of the richest in Russia, and the iron that came from these furnaces roofed churches, armed regiments, and built bridges across the empire. Ore came from the great iron mountain of Vysokaya, a hill that was dug away over centuries, leaving a vast pit, and the mining museum in the town has good displays on the old trade.

In the Soviet era, the city became a symbol of heavy industry. The Uralvagonzavod works, evacuated from Kharkiv in 1941, produced railway wagons and then T-34 tanks, which came to be known as the weapon that won the war, and the plant is still one of the biggest tank factories in the world. The skyline is a forest of chimneys, and the haze that hangs over the valley on a still day tells you what kind of place this is. About three hundred and eighty thousand people live here, in a long, narrow strip along the river.

Culture has a place too. The town is known for Tagil trays, painted metal trays decorated with bright flowers on a black background, a craft that began in the eighteenth century and is still practised. A museum shows the history of the tradition, and you can buy a small one as a souvenir.

The riding approach is mostly flat, with the Urals low and rounded around the town, and the road in from Yekaterinburg or Perm runs through forest and hills, with moderate traffic. Surfaces can be rough, with patching, and industrial lorries are common. Summers are warm, winters hard, and the best months are May to September. Smog can be an issue in still weather.

Fuel, food and beds are plentiful, with petrol stations on every main road, supermarkets, cafés, and hotels of varying quality. A day in the city is a day in the Urals' industrial heart, and it is not pretty, but it is real. Climb the viewpoint above the river if you can, and look over the roofs. It shows you what the Demidovs built.
t.kyshtym@55.7,60.6:
Kyshtym is a name that most people know from a disaster rather than from the town. In September 1957, a storage tank at the Mayak nuclear complex exploded, scattering radioactive material across the eastern Urals in what is still one of the worst nuclear accidents in history. The plant was secret, and the city that served it, now called Ozersk, did not appear on any map, so the accident was named after the nearest known place, which was Kyshtym. The town itself, about ten kilometres from the plant, was not at the centre of the contamination, and today it is an ordinary, rather pleasant small city of forty thousand, but the shadow of the name has never quite lifted. The Soviet authorities kept the accident secret for decades, and the first public acknowledgement came only in the late 1980s.

Away from that history, Kyshtym sits in a landscape of lakes. The area between Kyshtym and Miass is a chain of deep, clear bodies of water set among pine forests, low hills and granite outcrops, and many are popular for swimming, camping and fishing. The town grew around an ironworks and a copper smelter in the eighteenth century, and later became a centre for kaolin and clay. Its streets are tidy, with a lake at the centre and a railway line that has carried the Trans-Siberian traffic for over a century.

For a rider, the roads here are flat to rolling, running through forest and farmland, with moderate traffic and a mostly good surface on the main routes. The route between Chelyabinsk and Yekaterinburg passes through, and trucks are common. Side roads to the lakes are quieter, sometimes sandy, and often charming in summer, when the smell of pine and hot sand hangs in the air. Weather is typical for the Urals, with changeable skies and sudden storms in July, and long, cold winters.

If you stop here, you will find all the basics: several petrol stations on the main roads, shops, cafés and a couple of modest hotels. It is a practical stop, and the lakeside is pleasant for a rest. Avoid wandering into restricted areas near the nuclear zone, which are signposted, and check local advice if you plan to leave the main roads.

Sit by the lake for a quarter of an hour. It is a small, peaceful corner, and the history is something to keep in mind.
t.karabash@55.5,60.2:
Karabash was once on lists of the most polluted places on earth, and the hills around it still carry the scars. For most of the twentieth century, the copper smelter at the heart of the town poured sulphur dioxide and heavy metals into the air, killing the forest on the surrounding slopes and leaving bare, eroded, orange and grey hills that look like another planet. By the 1990s, the town had a notorious reputation, and in 2006, an environmental group named it among the dirtiest places in the world. The old smelter has since been shut down and replaced, and the town has been trying to recover, with replanting efforts on the hills. The change is gradual, but real.

The history of Karabash is one of mining. Gold was found in the area in the nineteenth century, and copper followed, and the settlement grew up around the works. About fifteen thousand people live here now, in a mix of old wooden houses and Soviet blocks, on the edge of a small lake. The town is not pretty, but it is honest, and the people are used to being the subject of curiosity. A small museum and a memorial to the workers sit in the centre.

What makes Karabash interesting for a rider is the contrast. A few kilometres away, the Southern Urals offer the opposite: clean lakes, pine woods, granite cliffs, and old mountains, and the famous Lake Turgoyak, one of the clearest in Russia, is not far. The roads here wind through low hills, with a mix of good tarmac and patched sections, and the traffic is moderate. To the east, the plain stretches away toward Chelyabinsk. The weather is changeable, with hot summers and cold winters, and in spring, the snow melts quickly and leaves mud.

Practical matters are straightforward. Karabash has petrol stations, shops, and cafés, and it is a handy place for a stop, though Kyshtym, about thirty-four kilometres off, is the bigger centre. Accommodation is limited, and most visitors stay in Miass or at the lakes. Dust from the old tailings can be a nuisance in dry weather, so keep windows and visors closed on windy days.

If you stop, look at the hills and think about what a century of industry can do. It is a strong lesson, and it is also a hopeful place, because trees are beginning to grow back.
t.mansaf caravanserai@38.3,62.8:
Out in the Karakum, the great black-sand desert that covers most of Turkmenistan, the old caravan route between Merv and Amul on the Amu Darya crossed some two hundred kilometres of sand, and along it, at intervals of a day's march, stood caravanserais where travellers could rest, water their animals and find shelter. The ruins of the Mansaf caravanserai lie on this route, a crumbling square of brick walls and gateways in an empty landscape of dunes and saxaul shrubs. They are part of the Silk Roads heritage of Central Asia, and the corridor is on Turkmenistan's list of sites proposed for UNESCO recognition.

Caravanserais like Mansaf were built from the eleventh century onwards, often by rulers wanting to promote trade, and their layout was standard: a courtyard surrounded by rooms for travellers, stables for camels and horses, and sometimes a mosque, all enclosed within thick walls with a single gateway. The Karakum is a harsh environment, with summer temperatures well over forty-five degrees and winter nights below freezing, and nearby, the Repetek reserve protects the desert ecosystem, with its sand dunes, saxaul forests and wildlife adapted to the extreme conditions.

Riding in Turkmenistan is tightly controlled. Foreign visitors need a visa, which can be difficult to obtain, and independent travel is often restricted, so most trips are organised through local agencies with a guide. Bringing your own motorcycle involves significant paperwork. The main road between Mary and Türkmenabat, which follows the old caravan route, is paved but can be in poor condition, with long straight stretches across the desert, sand drifts and occasional checkpoints. Distances between services are long.

Fuel is cheap in Turkmenistan, but stations can be few and far between in the desert, so fill up in Mary or Türkmenabat and carry extra.
