The Jesuits and the Guarani built towns with a central plaza, a church, workshops, schools and houses for families, and the Guarani, who were skilled in music, carving and building, filled the churches with baroque sculpture and played European instruments with great skill. Loreto even had a printing press, where books in the Guarani language were produced around 1700, among the earliest presses in this part of South America. The missions were suppressed when the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767, and the towns were abandoned, and the jungle took over. The ruins of Loreto and Santa Ana, a few kilometres apart, are part of the World Heritage listing of the Jesuit missions.

Misiones is a different Argentina. The soil is a deep red, the vegetation a thick subtropical green, and the air is heavy and warm, with sudden storms. Roads run through plantations of yerba mate, the shrub whose leaves make the national drink, and tea, with orange groves and forest in between. The main road, Route 12, links Posadas with Iguazu, and is mostly good, but local roads can be rough, and after heavy rain the red mud is slippery. Cattle and dogs are common on the road, and the heat in summer can be intense, with humidity that soaks your clothes. The best months are April to October, with milder temperatures.

The tiny village of Loreto has little in the way of services, and the closest fuel and a bigger choice of shops are at Gobernador Roca, seventeen kilometres away, and San Ignacio, home to the most famous of the ruins, is nearby. Carry water and insect repellent, and take care of the sun at midday. In the evening, a gourd of mate shared with local people, and a meal of grilled meat, cassava and chipa, a small cheese bread, make a satisfying finish.
t.kelte minara koshk@37.6,62.1:
Once there were few cities in the world as big as Merv. At its height, in the twelfth century, under the Seljuk sultans, the oasis city on the Murghab river, in the sands of what is now Turkmenistan, may have been the largest on the planet, with a population counted in the hundreds of thousands, libraries that Arab geographers praised and a position on the Silk Road between Persia and Central Asia. In 1221, the Mongols arrived, and the chroniclers say that the slaughter was beyond counting. The city never recovered its size, but the ruins, which cover a vast area of low walls, mounds and shattered brick, were listed as a World Heritage site in 1999.

A koshk, in this region, is a fortified house or pavilion, a defended country residence of the kind that wealthy families built on the edge of a city, and Kelte Minara is one of those in the Merv oasis. The oasis holds buildings from many centuries: the high mud-brick walls of Erk Kala, the oldest part of the city, the heavy tomb of Sultan Sanjar, topped with a great double dome, and the huge fortified farmhouses of Greater and Lesser Kyz Kala.

The setting is the Karakum desert, a flat, pale country of sand, scrub and irrigated fields, and the roads are long and straight, with distant dust devils and heat shimmer in summer. The temperature can exceed forty-five degrees from June to August, so the best times are spring and autumn, with mild, clear weather. Winter can be cold at night. Wind and drifting sand cover the road in places, and camels and sheep wander on to the carriageway. Turkmenistan is a tightly controlled country, with strict entry rules, and foreign visitors normally need a visa and an arranged itinerary or guide, so a self-guided ride needs planning well in advance.

Bayramaly, seven kilometres away, is a town of about seventy-five thousand people, and Mary, the regional capital, is close by, with fuel stations, shops and hotels. Fuel in Turkmenistan is very cheap, because it is subsidised, although supplies for foreigners can be restricted. Carry plenty of water, shade and sun protection when you walk the ruins, and take your time, as the scale of the site is hard to take in at once. In the evening, the light on the old walls turns them a glowing red-gold.
t.st anthony@51.4,-55.6:
At St Anthony the road runs out of Newfoundland, or nearly. This is the northern capital of the Great Northern Peninsula, a fishing port of about two thousand people facing the cold Atlantic and the Labrador current, and it has been a lifeline for the whole coast since the English doctor Wilfred Grenfell set up a hospital here in the early twentieth century. The Grenfell historic properties still stand, and the story of the doctor who sailed from cove to cove to treat fishing families is one of the best told in the province.

The ride up the Viking Trail on Route 430 is long, honest and surprisingly dramatic. The road leaves the Gulf of St. Lawrence at Port au Choix, runs beside the Long Range Mountains, and then crosses open bogs and stunted spruce, the so-called tuckamore, bent flat by the wind. It is mostly straight, with long gentle swells, so the thrill is in the weather and the space. Moose are the real hazard, and every local has a story of one. Do not ride at night, and on any evening run keep the speed well below what the straight road invites, because a moose is as tall as a bar stool and about as easy to see in the dusk.

St Anthony is the sensible place to fuel, eat and sleep before the last run on Route 436 to L'Anse aux Meadows, where Norse settlers built their turf huts around the year 1000. In late spring and early summer, icebergs drift down from Greenland and sit grounded in the bay off the headlands, white and blue, and the whales come in close in July. The headlands around the harbour are an easy place to watch for both, and locals will tell you where the bergs have grounded this week. The best seafood is simple: cod, shrimp, crab in season, and a mug of tea.

The wind off the bay is cold even in July, and fog is common, so carry a warm layer. The summer riding season is short, running roughly from June to September, and the north is quiet outside those months.
t.bukhara@39.8,64.5:
Bukhara is a city made of brick and memory, a trading hub on the Silk Road with a history of more than two thousand years, and its old centre is one of the best preserved in Central Asia. The Zeravshan River once watered the oasis around it, and the town's wealth came from carpets, silk, gold embroidery and its position between east and west. Genghis Khan's army burned much of it in 1220, but the city recovered and became a great centre of Islamic learning, with scores of madrasas and mosques.

The Kalon Minaret, a tapering tower of patterned brick about forty-five metres high, was built in 1127 and has dominated the skyline ever since. It is said that Genghis Khan, struck by its beauty, ordered it spared when his troops razed the city. Beside it stand a great mosque and a madrasa, and at night the minaret is lit golden against the dark sky. Nearby, the mausoleum of Ismail Samani, built in the tenth century, is a small, perfect cube of woven brick that stood buried in sand for centuries and so survived.

The Ark, a fortress-palace on a high mound, was the residence of the emirs of Bukhara for more than a thousand years. In 1842, two British officers, Colonel Charles Stoddart and Captain Arthur Conolly, were executed in the square in front of it by order of the emir, an episode in the Great Game between Britain and Russia. The pool of Lyab-i Hauz, shaded by old mulberry trees, is the heart of the old town, with tea houses around the edge where you can sit and watch the evening. Covered trading domes, built to shelter merchants, still house craft shops.

Riding here, the road from Samarkand crosses the flat, dusty plain, with irrigated fields, cotton and orchards giving way to desert. The surface is variable, with patches of damaged asphalt and sudden potholes, and heat in summer is intense, so start early and carry water. Fuel stations are not always supplied with petrol, so fill up when you can. In the city, the old quarter has narrow lanes and little parking, and a hotel with a courtyard where bikes can be locked is a sensible choice. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, and the golden light on the brick at sunset is one of the sights of Central Asia.
t.jesuit missions of la santisima trinidad:
The Jesuit mission of Santisima Trinidad de Parana lies on a low hill in southern Paraguay, in the department of Itapua, and the stone ruins that remain are some of the most atmospheric in South America. It was founded in 1706 as one of the reducciones, the mission towns in which Jesuit priests gathered the Guarani people into settled communities, and it grew into one of the largest. At its height, several thousand people lived here around a vast central plaza, with a great church, a cemetery, a school, workshops, a college and rows of houses. The red sandstone church, begun in the 1740s, was decorated with carved figures, including angels playing musical instruments, and parts of its facade and pulpit remain.

The Guarani brought skill to the mission. They became sculptors, painters, weavers and instrument makers, and the missions were famous for their music, with choirs and orchestras playing European baroque pieces on locally made violins and harps. The Jesuits were expelled from the Spanish colonies in 1767, and the mission towns fell into decline. Trinidad was abandoned and the stone was robbed for local buildings, but the church and some of the surrounding buildings survived. The site was added to the UNESCO list in 1993, together with the nearby mission of Jesus de Tavarangue.

Itapua is farming country of red earth, soybeans, cassava and yerba mate. The roads are good, with Route 6 linking Encarnacion, the main city on the Parana River, to Ciudad del Este, and the mission sits off the highway on a smaller road. The air is hot and humid from November to March, and the red dust gets everywhere in the dry season. Thunderstorms can be violent in summer and turn dirt roads to slippery clay.

Hohenau, about nine kilometres away, is a settlement founded by German and other European immigrants at the start of the twentieth century. It has a distinctly central European feel, with German-named shops and bakeries, and it is a good place to eat and refuel. Trinidad has a few basic services. Drink tereré, the cold yerba mate that Paraguayans carry in a thermos everywhere, and eat sopa paraguaya, a dense cornbread that is not a soup at all.

Visit in late afternoon, when the sandstone glows red and the light is soft.
t.timurid iwans or askhab@37.7,62.2:
Just outside the town of Bayramaly in Turkmenistan's Mary region lies the biggest archaeological landscape in Central Asia, the oasis of Merv. People have farmed here since the Bronze Age, thanks to the Murghab river, which fans out into the Karakum desert and makes a green island in a sea of sand. Over the centuries, Merv became a great Silk Road city, called Mary or Marw, and at its height in the twelfth century under the Seljuk sultans it was one of the largest cities in the world. Then, in 1221, the Mongols came, and the chroniclers wrote of enormous slaughter. The city never recovered its former glory.

The name on the checkpoint comes from Askhab, an Arabic word meaning companions, a term for the companions of the Prophet Muhammad. Sites bearing that name in the Merv oasis are tied to the early Islamic centuries, when this was a base for the Arab conquest of the east, and later buildings in the area carry Timurid-style iwans, the tall vaulted portals typical of Central Asian architecture. The scale is not like Samarkand's. These are brick structures weathered by wind and heat, but the arches stand against a pale sky in a way that is quietly moving.

Riding to Merv from the town of Mary takes you through flat irrigated land, with cotton fields, canals and poplar lines, and the road is generally straight and decently surfaced. The Karakum is close, and dust, heat and wind are a normal part of the ride, so a scarf and plenty of water are not luxuries. Spring, when the steppe is briefly green, and autumn are far more pleasant than the summer months, when temperatures often pass forty. Riding in Turkmenistan involves paperwork and frequent police checkpoints, so check entry rules, route permissions and insurance with care beforehand.

Bayramaly is a sizeable town of about seventy-five thousand and has fuel, bread and tea houses, and the city of Mary, thirty kilometres on, is better still. Petrol in Turkmenistan has long been cheap, but supplies and rules for foreigners change, so do not assume. Walk the ruins in early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is gentle and the mud brick glows.
t.mausoleum of imam qasim@37.7,62.2:
Some places in Merv are enormous and some are intimate, and this belongs to the second kind. The mausoleum of Imam Qasim is a small pilgrimage site in the oasis, a place for quiet prayer rather than spectacle, the sort of shrine that has drawn local visitors for a very long time. It sits in the broad landscape of Merv, east of the Karakum desert, within a few kilometres of the town of Bayramaly, and the contrast between the quiet shrine and the huge empty ruins nearby is a big part of its character.

For anyone arriving by motorcycle, the surroundings are the lesson. The oasis is flat, so the road is straight and unhurried, running between cotton fields, drainage channels and rows of poplar and mulberry. Further out the cultivated land stops abruptly, as if cut with a knife, and the pale desert begins. That edge is the whole story of the Murghab delta. Heat is the main challenge, with summers frequently touching forty degrees and the wind carrying fine dust, so pick the cooler months, and keep water and shade in mind. Dawn rides are magical here, with long shadows on the earth and the air still cool.

The history is deep. Islam arrived in Merv in the seventh century, when Arab armies took the city and used it as a base for pushing east. Within a few generations it became a famous centre of learning, with libraries said to hold huge numbers of books, and scholars such as the geographer Yaqut passed through before the Mongol destruction in 1221. Pilgrimage traditions grew around the tombs of holy figures, and Turkmen families still visit them to pray, tie cloths and leave small offerings. If you go, dress modestly, remove your shoes where asked, and be quiet. Photography is best done with permission.

For fuel and food, Bayramaly, a town of roughly seventy-five thousand, is the nearest dependable source, and Mary is larger still. Nothing at the shrine itself should be expected, apart perhaps from a seller of water or sweets on a busy day. Carry cash in local currency, and be prepared for checkpoints and questions along the road. A calm, patient attitude works wonders.
t.l anse aux meadows@51.6,-55.5:
At the very top of Newfoundland's Northern Peninsula, where the land ends in low, windy moorland and the cold water of the Strait of Belle Isle, a handful of grassy mounds mark the only confirmed Norse settlement in North America. L'Anse aux Meadows was found in 1960 by the Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad and his wife, the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad, following local directions to some strange humps beside the bay, and excavation showed eight buildings of turf and timber from about the year 1000. It was one of the first places in the world to be placed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, in 1978.

The site is looked after by Parks Canada, and reconstructed sod houses stand near the original foundations, with costumed staff who show how the Norse smelted iron and lived through the winter. The buildings are small and smoky and very quiet, and the wind here has a way of making the whole story seem very close. Nobody knows whether this was the Vinland of the sagas or a base for exploring, but it was clearly a place where people lived and worked, and it proves that Europeans crossed the Atlantic five hundred years before Columbus.

The Viking Trail, as Route 430 and 436 are known, runs for hundreds of kilometres north from Deer Lake past Gros Morne National Park and along the Gulf of St Lawrence. The road is generally good, with long straight stretches and wide views of the sea on one side and low spruce and bog on the other. Moose are a constant danger, especially at dusk and dawn, and every rider should slow down and watch the verges. Fog can roll in from the cold water without warning.

For fuel, the last real town before the end is St. Anthony, about twenty-five kilometres away, and it is the sensible place to fill up and eat. The site and surrounding villages have a few small restaurants and guesthouses, but services thin out the further north you go, and the season is short, with the site open only from roughly early June to early October.

In early summer, icebergs drift down from Greenland along this coast, and they can be seen from the headlands, glowing white against the grey sea. Dress warmly even in July.
t.yekaterinburg@56.8,60.6:
Yekaterinburg is a big, confident city on the eastern side of the Ural Mountains, at the point where Europe is supposed to end and Asia to begin, and it behaves as if it knew its own importance. It was founded in 1723 as an ironworking fortress by two engineers sent by Peter the Great, and named after his wife, later Empress Catherine I. The Iset river, dammed in the middle of the city to power the original factory, still forms a pond called the Plotinka in the city centre.

Wealth from iron, copper and gemstones built the city. The Urals are rich in minerals, and the mines nearby produced malachite, emeralds, amethysts and gold, and the city's stonecutting and jewellery traditions continue. The famous Demidov family built a fortune on the ironworks of this region, and their route from here north toward Nizhny Tagil follows the old industrial centres.

The history is not only about industry. In July 1918, the last Tsar, Nicholas II, and his family were executed in the cellar of a merchant's house here, and the Church on the Blood now stands on the spot, a large, ornate building with golden domes. The site draws a stream of visitors, and the story remains emotional for many Russians. The city also has some excellent constructivist architecture from the 1920s and 1930s, with bold geometric buildings that remain striking.

The border between Europe and Asia is marked by an obelisk on the old Siberian road, west of the city, where visitors pose with one foot in each continent. The geography here is gentler than the symbolism: the Urals are old, eroded mountains, only a thousand metres or so high, and in this latitude they look like forested hills.

The roads around Yekaterinburg are mixed. The ring road and main highways are busy with trucks, and the city's traffic can be heavy and aggressive, with slow rush hours. Beyond, the lanes through the hills are pleasant, with lakes, pine woods and granite outcrops, though surfaces can be broken, and frost heaves are common after the long winter.

Fuel, food and every service are available in the city, and it is a good place to restock before the Urals or Siberia. The local food includes pelmeni, small dumplings served with sour cream and vinegar, which the region claims as its own. Summer is warm and short, autumn is bright, and winter is long and cold.
t.miass@55.0,60.1:
Miass is a southern Urals city set in a wide valley between the Ilmen mountains and the long ridge of the Urals, and it is famous in Russia for two reasons: gold and trucks. Gold was found in the river sands here in the 1770s, and in the 1840s one of the largest nuggets ever found in Russia, known as the Big Triangle, was dug up near the town. It weighed about thirty-six kilograms and is now kept in the Diamond Fund in Moscow. Today the city's best-known product is the Ural truck, built at a factory that was moved here from Moscow in 1941, and the heavy trucks have crossed the roughest roads of the Soviet Union.

The landscape is the real attraction. To the south of the city lies the Ilmen Nature Reserve, created in 1920 as the first mineralogical reserve in the world, an area of low granite hills, lakes and pine forest that contains an extraordinary range of minerals, many of them found nowhere else. Geologists and mineral collectors have come here for two centuries, and a museum in the town displays some of the finds. To the west, Lake Turgoyak, about twelve kilometers from the city, is a deep, clear lake surrounded by pine-covered rocks, sometimes called the Little Baikal for its transparency and depth.

For riders, the roads around Miass are some of the best in the region. The route to Zlatoust, over the Ural ridge, climbs through forest with bends and views, and the road from Kyshtym and Karabash passes through landscapes shaped by the mining industry, some of them bleak and some stunning. The surface is a mix of good and poor, and traffic is moderate. The weather is changeable, with warm summer days and thunderstorms, a beautiful golden autumn and a long, snowy winter. The best months are June to September.

Services are very good. With about a hundred and sixty thousand people, Miass has fuel stations, shops, cafes and several hotels, and Turgoyak has small guesthouses and cafes in summer. It is the place to stock up before heading into the hills.

Swim in Turgoyak if the weather allows. The water is cold and astonishingly clear, and the pines on the shore are thick with resin.
